title: Projectile Motion
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Two Motions Wearing One Body

A projectile is free fall with a head start: uniform horizontal velocity (a = 0) superposed on vertical free fall (a = g). Because the components are independent, the whole parabolic story unfolds from two one-dimensional problems sharing one clock.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Projectile launched at angle θ with speed u (level ground)

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Horizontal component | $u_x = u\cos\theta$ (constant throughout) |
| Vertical component | $u_y = u\sin\theta$ (changes by g) |
| Time to maximum height | $t_{up} = u\sin\theta/g$ |
| **Time of flight** | $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$ |
| **Maximum height** | $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$ |
| **Horizontal range** | $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ |
| Trajectory | parabola: $y = x\tan\theta - gx^2/2u^2\cos^2\theta$ |

**Key results:**
- $R$ is maximum at **θ = 45°** ($R_{max} = u^2/g$).
- Complementary angles (θ and 90° − θ) give the **same range** — $R(30°) = R(60°)$; ratio 1:1.
- Range ratio for two angles: $R_1/R_2 = \sin2\theta_1/\sin2\theta_2$.

### 2.2 Horizontal projection from a height

A body projected horizontally with speed u from height h:
- **Time of flight:** $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ (depends only on h).
- **Horizontal range:** $R = u\sqrt{2h/g}$.
- **Velocity on striking:** $v = \sqrt{u^2 + 2gh}$ at angle $\tan\alpha = \sqrt{2gh}/u$ below horizontal.

### 2.3 Vertical projection

$T = 2u/g$, $H = u^2/2g$ (Topic 9's results).

## 3. Worked Numericals

**Q1 (3m, 2024):** A body is projected with velocity 20 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find its maximum height and horizontal range. (g = 10 m/s²)
*Given:* u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°.
*Substitution:* $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g = 400 \times 0.25/20 = 5$ m.
$R = u^2\sin2\theta/g = 400 \times \sin60°/10 = 40 \times 0.866 = 34.6$ m.
*Answer:* **H = 5 m, R ≈ 34.6 m.**

**Q2 (5m, 2022):** A projectile is fired horizontally from a tower 80 m high with velocity 20 m/s. Find (i) time of flight, (ii) horizontal range, (iii) velocity on striking the ground. (g = 10 m/s²)
*Substitution:* (i) $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ s.
(ii) $R = ut = 20 \times 4 = 80$ m.
(iii) $v_y = gt = 40$ m/s; $v = \sqrt{u^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{400 + 1600} = \sqrt{2000} = 44.7$ m/s at $\tan\alpha = 40/20 = 2 → \alpha = 63.4°$ below horizontal.
*Answer:* **t = 4 s, R = 80 m, v ≈ 44.7 m/s at 63.4° below horizontal.**

**Q3 (4m, 2022):** A stone is projected vertically upwards with 49 m/s (g = 9.8). Find time to maximum height, maximum height, total time.
$t_{up} = u/g = 5$ s; $H = u^2/2g = 122.5$ m; $T = 2u/g = 10$ s.

## 4. Derivation asked at NEB (2019, 2022)

**Time of flight is double the time to maximum height (3m, 2019):**
At maximum height the vertical velocity vanishes: $0 = u\sin\theta - gt_{up} → t_{up} = u\sin\theta/g$. The projectile lands when the vertical displacement returns to zero: $0 = u\sin\theta\,T - \frac{1}{2}gT^2 → T = 2u\sin\theta/g$. Hence **T = 2 t_up** — the flight is symmetric about the highest point.

**Range is the same for complementary angles (3m, 2022):**
$R = \frac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$. For θ and (90° − θ): $\sin2(90°-\theta) = \sin(180° - 2\theta) = \sin2\theta$ — identical. So $R(30°) = R(60°)$; **the ratio of ranges for 30° and 60° is 1:1**.

## 5. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 4 (resolution):** the whole topic is resolution in action — $u\cos\theta$ and $u\sin\theta$ start two independent problems.
- **To Topic 9:** the vertical half is free fall; the horizontal half is uniform velocity.
- **To Energy:** speed at any height follows from energy conservation — $v^2 = u^2 - 2gy$.
- **To real life:** ballistics, water fountains, javelin throws and fire hoses all obey $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$.

### 6.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Using $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin2\theta$ in the range formula.
2. Applying $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$ to horizontal projection — there $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$.
3. Mixing components: horizontal velocity never changes; vertical velocity never stays.
4. Forgetting that maximum range needs 45° only on **level ground**.
5. In horizontal-projection numericals, using u in the vertical equations.

specificConditions: **Independence of Components:** Horizontal motion (constant $v_x = u\cos	heta$) and vertical motion (free fall $v_y = u\sin	heta - gt$) are completely independent. They share only the time variable $t$. This is the foundational principle — no horizontal force means $v_x$ is constant.

**Trajectory is a Parabola:** Eliminating $t$ gives $y = x	an	heta -  rac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2	heta}$, a downward-opening parabola. This assumes no air resistance, constant $g$, and flat ground. With drag, the trajectory is not a parabola and range decreases.

**Symmetry and Range Maxima:** Time of flight $T =  rac{2u\sin	heta}{g}$, max height $H =  rac{u^2\sin^2	heta}{2g}$, range $R =  rac{u^2\sin 2	heta}{g}$. Maximum range at $	heta = 45^\circ$. Complementary angles ($	heta$ and $90^\circ-	heta$) give identical ranges because $\sin 2	heta = \sin(180^\circ-2	heta)$. Speed at launch = speed at landing (symmetry).
